charts.title: Two ways to hold data out, and a planted data set with nothing to learn that tells them apart.
charts.takeaway: With nothing to learn, a random split over windows still reads 1.000 and a held-out-person split reads 0.469: the random split scores memory of each person.

steps.label: 2,122 windows, 15 people
steps.detail: WESAD chest recordings cut into windows. 30 percent are stress windows.

steps.label: Random split over windows
steps.detail: Windows from one person land in both the training and the test set.

steps.label: Held-out-person split
steps.detail: Each person is tested by a model trained only on the other people.

steps.label: Planted: nothing to learn
steps.detail: Each block gets its own offset and the label carries no shared signal. Random split 1.000, held-out person 0.469.

steps.label: Control: block shuffle
steps.detail: The stress label moves to a random condition block in each person, 100 draws. 95th percentile 0.656.

steps.label: Rule: gap of at least 0.02
steps.detail: The random split must read at least 0.02 above the held-out-person split for the forest. Set before any label was compared.

steps.label: Gap 0.033
steps.detail: Real data, random forest: 1.000 random, 0.966 held-out person.

charts.title: The same model scored two ways: random split over windows against a held-out person.
charts.takeaway: The random split reads higher every time: by 0.033 for the forest, 0.086 for logistic regression, and 0.531 on planted data that holds nothing to learn.
charts.units: AUC (area under the ROC curve: the chance a stress window scores above a calm one; 0.5 is chance, 1 is perfect), pooled over all held-out windows; higher is better
charts.n: 2,122 windows from 15 people; second run on a new seed gave the forest 0.999 and 0.966
charts.no_interval: The result file holds one pooled AUC per model and split. The within-person interval for the forest is in the next chart.
charts.baseline: Chance is 0.5. Block-shuffle control for logistic regression on held-out people: mean 0.487, 95th percentile 0.656
charts.threshold: Gap of at least 0.02 for the forest (held, 0.033); planted data at least 0.8 under the random split and at most 0.6 for a held-out person (both held)
charts.planted: Nothing to learn: 1.000 random split, 0.469 held-out person

charts.takeaway: The forest holds for every person (lowest 0.912, S2; mean 0.979), while logistic regression drops to 0.646 for S15.

charts.title: Which sensors carry stress to a person the model has not seen.
charts.takeaway: Physiology without motion or breath reaches 0.97 for a held-out person; motion alone (acceleration with EMG) reaches 0.79.
charts.units: AUC within a held-out person, mean over people, random forest (0.5 is chance, 1 is perfect); higher is better
charts.n: 2,122 windows from 15 people; 100 block permutations per sensor group for the q values
charts.no_interval: The result file holds one mean AUC per sensor group and a corrected q value from the logistic permutation test, with no interval.
charts.threshold: Physiology above motion, set in advance: held, 0.97 against 0.79

axis.label: AUC for a held-out person (0.5 is chance)

charts.title: Did people who reported a larger rise in anxiety also change more in the body?
charts.takeaway: No link shows: rank correlation 0.03 with EDA, 0.02 with heart rate and −0.45 with breathing rate (p 0.090).
charts.units: Spearman rho (a rank correlation from −1 to 1; 0 is no relation) between the rise in reported anxiety and the bodily change, across people
charts.n: 15 people; reported anxiety (six-item STAI) rose by 7.7 points on average
charts.no_interval: The result file holds rho and its p value for each signal, with no interval. With 15 people an interval on rho is wide.
charts.ruled_out: Only a strong positive relation. The largest rho is 0.03, and 15 people cannot rule out a moderate one.
